title: POEMS: End-to-End Performance Design of Large Parallel Adaptive Computational Systems
extended_summary:
This paper does not match the requested 2025 secondary-education AI writing-feedback study. Instead, it is a computer systems and software engineering paper describing the POEMS (Performance Oriented End-to-end Modeling System) project, which addresses the problem of how to model and predict the performance of large parallel and distributed computational systems across application software, runtime/operating system software, and hardware architecture. The paper focuses on methodology for composing models from multiple domains, at multiple levels of detail, using different paradigms such as analysis, simulation, and direct measurement.

The approach proposed is an end-to-end performance modeling framework built around generalized dependence graphs, compositional objects with associative interfaces, a POEMS Specification Language (PSL), a database of component models and performance data, and supporting tools such as task-graph generators, analytic models, and simulators. The paper demonstrates these ideas using the Sweep3D benchmark application, showing how analytical and simulation models can be integrated to predict performance under alternative hardware and software configurations. The emphasis is on system design methodology rather than on human learners, instruction, or educational outcomes.

No educational population is studied. The paper concerns computational workloads and benchmark applications executed on parallel architectures such as IBM SP/2 and SGI Origin 2000, with contributions from researchers across several universities in the United States and the United Kingdom. There are no students, teachers, schools, or educational settings involved.

The main conclusion is that POEMS offers a conceptual and technical framework for composing multidomain, multiparadigm, and multiresolution performance models into coherent end-to-end system models. The authors argue that this can support more effective performance prediction and design exploration for complex parallel systems. Based on the supplied text alone, the requested education study is not found here and is likely mis-cited, conflated with another paper, or absent/unpublished in the source used for retrieval.
